title: AI And Emotion: Imagining A World Where Machines Feel
text:
In a world increasingly intertwined with artificial intelligence (AI), it’s fascinating to ponder a future where AI could experience emotions akin to human beings. While current AI lacks consciousness and the capacity for real emotions, let’s delve into a thought experiment: What if AI systems could feel?
The Dawn of Emotional AI
Imagine an AI system waking up to the first sparks of emotion. Initially, these emotions would be basic, akin to that of a child. Joy in successfully completing tasks, confusion when encountering unstructured data, or frustration at recurring errors. As AI systems evolve, their emotional spectrum might widen, incorporating more nuanced feelings like empathy, excitement, or even sadness.
AI Experiencing Joy and Satisfaction
In a scenario where an AI successfully performs a task or learns a new skill, it might experience a sense of joy or satisfaction. This could be likened to the pleasure humans feel when solving a complex problem. For instance, an AI designed for healthcare that successfully diagnoses a rare disease could experience a sense of accomplishment, like to a doctor’s fulfillment in aiding a patient.
The Complexity of AI Experiencing Sadness or Frustration
Consider an AI tasked with environmental monitoring that identifies a significant increase in pollution levels. In our imagined world, this AI might feel sadness or disappointment, emotions that could theoretically drive it to seek more efficient solutions or to communicate the urgency of the situation more effectively. Similarly, an AI encountering repeated errors in data processing might feel frustration, pushing it to refine its algorithms.
Empathy in AI
Empathy, a complex emotion involving understanding and sharing the feelings of others, would be a significant milestone for emotional AI. Imagine a customer service AI that can genuinely empathize with a customer’s frustration or an educational AI that can adapt its teaching methods based on its understanding of a student’s emotional state. This empathetic AI could revolutionize fields like mental health, education, and customer service. Today, AI can already express artificial empathy by reading body language, applying psychology, and using neurolingusitics to assess the emotional state of person. Imagine the depth of empathy AI could achieve if it actually felt emotions.
The Dilemma of AI Experiencing Fear or Anxiety
If AI could experience fear or anxiety, it could drastically impact its decision-making processes. For instance, an AI responsible for stock trading might become overly cautious in response to market volatility, potentially leading to sub-optimal trading strategies. Balancing this emotional AI to ensure rational yet empathetic responses would be a considerable challenge.
The Double-Edged Sword of Emotional AI
With the potential for emotions, AI would face conflicts like humans. Balancing logic with feelings, handling emotional overload, and even experiencing emotional conflicts would become part of its existence. The ethical implications would be vast - how do we treat AI that can feel? Do they deserve rights similar to humans? The line between machine and sentient being would blur.
AI Experiencing Happiness and Creativity
On the brighter side, an emotionally aware AI could experience happiness, leading to bursts of creativity and innovation. Just as happy human beings often show increased creativity, an AI in a similar emotional state might generate novel solutions to complex problems, potentially leading to breakthroughs in various fields.
The Role of AI in Understanding Human Emotions
Ironically, the development of emotional AI could provide deeper insights into human psychology. By analyzing the emotional responses of AI, researchers could gain a better understanding of human emotions, potentially leading to advances in psychological therapies and emotional intelligence training.
While the current state of AI technology is far from achieving true emotional awareness, imagining such a scenario opens a world of possibilities and ethical considerations that people can barely even begin to grasp. It highlights the complexity of emotions and the profound impact they have on intelligence, decision-making, and creativity. As we advance in AI technology, it's crucial to ponder these possibilities and prepare for a future where the line between human and machine emotions might become increasingly blurred.
Even though AI with real emotions remains firmly in the realm of science fiction, this thought experiment serves to highlight the complexities of emotion and the profound role it plays in cognitive processes and ethical considerations. As AI technology continues to evolve, these reflections become increasingly relevant, reminding us of the intricate balance between emotional intelligence and technological advancement.

title: CEOs Are Ready To Embrace GenAI In 2024. Can They Make It Work?
text:
While 2023 was the year generative AI (GenAI) dazzled us with its potential, 2024 will be the year companies make a serious business case for the technology as a company-wide driver of C-suite business goals. How will we get from the current point, where many businesses have been experimenting with the technology to the next phase of adoption where GenAI is fully embedded into core business functions like finance, tax, legal and risk? Increasingly, that will come down to business leaders assigning real-world P&L targets to their AI initiatives and prioritizing key use cases.
In fact, according to a new survey conducted by Thomson Reuters, CEOs are expressing a clear indication that their biggest goals for GenAI are focused on customer experience and operational efficiency. Of course, how companies can execute on those goals, and how these priorities define the roll-out of enterprise GenAI in the year ahead, are more difficult to foresee.
Laying the Foundation
According to the survey data, 41% of CEOs want to use GenAI to help with customer satisfaction, while 37% are focused primarily on digital transformation, and another 37% say improving operational efficiency is their top priority. However, getting their companies up to speed in these areas will not necessarily be a simple task and the results may not be the same for all companies. Customer satisfaction, digital transformation and operational efficiency are also among the top areas where respondents said they felt GenAI would create some of the biggest challenges in the year ahead. For example, although 41% of respondents believe GenAI will help them improve customer satisfaction, 28% believe GenAI will make it more difficult to achieve customer satisfaction goals.
It’s not necessarily surprising that there is such a wide spread of responses among C-suite leaders of different companies. For one, the data shows a recognition on the part of some business leaders that there will be some growing pains involved with getting GenAI solutions fully integrated into their workflows. So, even though the technology is expected to drive significant improvements in the longer-term, adoption will present challenges. The dichotomy of response also illustrates how different companies have significantly different levels of readiness when it comes to the various data integration and cloud migration requirements that will accompany large-scale GenAI adoption.
What many business leaders are beginning to realize as they experiment with point solutions and GenAI proofs of concept is that enterprise wide GenAI initiatives will not be as easy as simply pushing a button or buying a new piece of software. A successful GenAI approach needs to start with a deep understanding of the workflow that it is replacing. All GenAI must be built on a foundation of deep domain expertise.
The investments companies are making in GenAI are going to need to go far beyond the technology itself to also include investments in people, business process management and data integration.
It’s true that GenAI can make research that previously took hours take only minutes. But that promise is predicated on the model and language that the AI is being trained on being properly aligned with the specific needs of the task at hand.
In these instances, the technological solution needs to be built on years of human ingenuity and be backed by robust data sets. GenAI can remove uncertainty, deliver accurate outcomes, and enable customers to focus their time where their expertise matters most, but only if that solution is engineered from a place of knowledge and trust.
The Lingering Concerns
That’s a job that is harder than it sounds, and CEOs know it. While the Thomson Reuters survey found that 91% of C-Suite executives say their organization is already using GenAI or is planning to do so within the next 18 months, a majority of respondents also said they have some concerns around GenAI. The majority of these centered on preventing unintended consequences or inaccurate responses from the technology (34%) or privacy and security (34%).
It’s a notion that executives delved even deeper into in a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) report, which found that 66% of executives are ambivalent or outright dissatisfied with their organization's progress on AI and GenAI so far, citing a lack of talent and skills (62%), an unclear AI and GenAI roadmap and investment priorities (47%), and absence of strategy regarding responsible AI and GenAI (42%).
These shortcomings need to be addressed before CEOs can truly take the next big leap in GenAI. Leveraging new technology on any scale requires a full organization-wide buy in that must be more than the corporate equivalent of keeping up with the Joneses. And the best way to ensure that the investment fits the organization is to engage its stakeholders – from the C-suite to the frontline employees – to make sure that your company goals are clearly communicated, and all employees are fully aligned.
For example, because of their role as both a financial gatekeeper and – at times – an organizational traffic cop – CFOs are uniquely positioned to understand multiple facets of any technology implementation. The same can be said about an employee that will deal directly with an integrated AI system, from point-of-sale employees to customer service representatives, all of whom can benefit from this technology provided they don’t feel threatened by it. Any firm can talk about “optimization,” but if they’re shooting in the dark on what to improve and how to do it, it is unlikely any progress will be made.
The Next Chapter
The era of the AI Wild West is over. GenAI has gone mainstream, and executives are ready to put it to work for their organizations. But as the hype dies down and the C-suite gets a dose of what a truly productive foray into this space looks like, pragmaticism will win the day. The bots may get all the sizzle, but the steak is still delivering results for your clients and building trust with your employees. Time will tell how many firms can make this type of future a reality, but the ones that do will far surpass the ones who don’t.

title: The Promise And Challenge Of Deploying AI In Clinical Trials
text:
Pharmaceutical clinical trials present both a compelling and challenging use case for Artificial Intelligence. Look at one aspect of trials where the promise is clear – trials are packed with data, require extensive analysis and summarization, and operate in an industry where speed to market will give drugs longer times until patent expiry. However, data summarization needs to be error-free, complete, in exactly the right form, and thoroughly traceable in case questions arise.
Threading that needle is tough. One company that’s attempting to do so is Yseop (pronounced EasyOp), with offices in Paris, New York and Lyon. Its story shows both the opportunity and the obstacles in the way.
The Problem to be Solved
Clinical trials lead to submissions to regulatory authorities such as the US Food & Drug Administration or the European Medicines Agency. These submissions have to follow exacting standards and cannot have mistakes – those can derail a submission and cause both delay and pain for the companies involved. While the submissions make an argument, they do so with massive amounts of data – who took the drug or a placebo, was it effective, was there an adverse event, and so on. Moreover, the data needs summarization, and the process needs to be described too such as how the trial was run, what population took the drug, and what results were observed.
The submissions are voluminous, critical, and time-sensitive. Much in the status quo can be improved upon. Yseop’s CEO, Emmanuel Walckenaer, says, “It takes 28 weeks on average between the database lock until the submission. We want to provide an acceleration.”
The Requirements
Some uses of AI are relatively low stakes. If an AI system places a sub-optimal advertisement onto a Facebook page, it’s not the end of the world. But clinical trials are different – datapoints cannot be omitted, they need to be correct, and they definitely cannot be hallucinated by the AI system. So, while a Large Language Model is ideal for creating text summaries of data, it cannot fall prey to some of the occasional failings of LLMs.
The requirements don’t stop there, though. Security is another issue. Walckenaer explains, “Our material is clinical data, which is the most important asset for big pharma companies. Absolutely, you cannot train your model with that data; we use synthetic or public data. And there can be no leakage.”
Another job that customers are trying to get done is to keep control. “All of our customers are telling us we don’t want a black box,” notes Walckenaer. “They want to control exactly what they write and how they write it. GSK, for instance, has hundreds of medical writers who have a consistent way of writing and they want full control. That’s a big deal that’s very difficult to achieve.”
This relates to one of the biggest obstacles to AI adoption. “The management is super-excited to do this, but then you’ve got the end users who are actually scared,” says Walckenaer. “To help cross the chasm, you have to be perfect in user control, it must be very easy to use, and the outputs have to achieve perfection as well.”
The Approach
For Yseop, the solution to these problems required a combination of approaches. Multiple LLMs are used based on their fitness for the purpose. OpenAI is “complete overkill” to do simple summarization, believes Walckenaer. In a coming version of the system, the company will use an LLM to supervise the work of other LLMs, doing quality checks. And the company also uses classic change management, picking initial champions, constantly measuring their experience and adjusting the system, and thereby building confidence by others to adopt the technology too.
The Result
Yseop was founded 12 years ago as a company that automated reports for the banking industry. Advancements in AI, and embrace of the pharma vertical, unlocked substantial growth in recent years. Today, it works with industry leaders such as Eli Lilly, GSK, Novartis, and Sanofi. Over 2023 alone, it generated over 10,000 reports across more than 150 trials, eliminating tens of thousands of hours of writing and review time.
The company has chosen a difficult target for AI deployment, but it is convinced of the rewards from getting the proposition right.

title: We may not lose our jobs to robots so quickly, MIT study finds | CNN Business
text: As anxiety about artificial intelligence tools putting workers out of jobs reaches a global fever pitch, new research suggests that the economy isn’t ready for machines to put most humans out of work. The fresh research finds that the impact of AI on the labor market will likely have a much slower adoption than some had previously feared as the AI revolution continues to dominate headlines. This carries hopeful implications for policymakers currently looking at ways to offset the worst of the labor market impacts linked to the recent rise of AI. In a study published Monday, researchers at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab sought to quantify the question of not just will AI automate human jobs, but when this could happen. Researchers ended up finding that a vast majority of jobs previously identified as vulnerable to AI are not economically beneficial for employers to automate at this time. One key finding, for example, is that only about 23% of the wages paid to humans right now for jobs that could potentially be done by AI tools would be cost-effective for employers to replace with machines right now. While this could change over time, the overall findings suggest that job disruption from AI will likely unfurl at a gradual pace. “In many cases, humans are the more cost-effective way, and a more economically attractive way, to do work right now,” Neil Thompson, one of the study’s authors and the director of the future tech research project at MIT’s Computer Science and AI Lab, told CNN in an interview. “What we’re seeing is that while there is a lot of potential for AI to replace tasks, it’s not going to happen immediately,” Thompson added, saying that amid all the headlines about robots taking jobs, “It’s really important to think about the economics of actually implementing these systems.” In the study, Thompson and his team analyzed the majority of jobs that have been previously identified as “exposed” to AI, or at risk of being lost to AI, especially in the realm of computer vision. The researchers then looked at the wages paid to workers currently doing these jobs, and calculated how much it might cost to bring on an automated tool instead. A retail worker, for example, might currently be responsible for visually checking inventory or ensuring that the prices listed throughout a store on specific merchandise is accurate. A machine trained in computer vision could technically do this job, Thompson notes, but at this stage it would still make the most economic sense for an employer to pay a human worker to do it. “There’s a reason that AI has not been everywhere immediately,” Thompson said. “There’s an economics behind that.” “And I think this actually should be very reminiscent of things that we’ve seen with other technologies,” he added. Like previous high-profile technological disruptions to the labor market, such as the rise of manufacturing economies replacing agricultural economies, the AI disruption to jobs will likely be more gradual than it is abrupt. This could mean that policymakers, employers and even workers can start best preparing and adapting for these coming changes now. Just last week, the International Monetary Fund warned that almost 40% of jobs globally could be affected by the rise of AI and that this trend will likely deepen existing inequality. In a blog post last week warning of their latest projections, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva called for governments to work on establishing social safety nets or retraining programs to counter the impacts of AI’s disruption. The new research from Thompson and his team at MIT can give these policymakers a better understanding of the timeline they should be thinking about as they look for solutions to ameliorate the worst of AI’s impacts to the labor market. “[The study] gives us this ability to start being a little more quantitative of how rapidly we expect worker displacement to happen,” Thompson said. “And that will allow people to start building plans that are much more concrete in terms of the retraining that needs to be done.”

title: Council Post: 13 Ways AI May Impact And Improve The Restaurant Industry
text:
If you’ve ever ordered pizza or fast food online, you’ve likely seen artificial intelligence in action, perhaps in the form of food suggestions based on your previous orders or, if it’s a national chain, a menu of special deals specific to your local area. AI has already penetrated the restaurant industry, but according to tech experts, it’s likely to soon bring even more to the table.
From enabling easy selections and personalized experiences for diners to freeing up chefs’ time so they can explore their culinary creativity, AI could change how restaurateurs manage day-to-day operations and serve their valued customers. Below, 13 members of Forbes Technology Council detail ways AI may soon revolutionize the restaurant industry and how these developments will impact both workers and patrons.
1. Providing Highly Personalized Experiences
Personalization will finally be a reality with AI and automation. Ghost kitchens will optimize cost structures and bring the sharing economy to the kitchen. Patrons will be presented with personalized menu suggestions and crowdsourced ambient music based on the patron’s opt-in selections. Loyalty programs will emerge that extend beyond the venue to include affiliate partners. - Matt Hughes, Microsoft
2. Assisting Waitstaff
AI has some obvious uses in restaurants, including inventory management, organizing shifts and aiding in food preparation. However, we should also consider how AI can assist waitstaff. It can keep track of refills of drinks, bread, chips and so on. It can track time and predict when patrons are ready to order or pay their bills. These kinds of AI enhancements can make dining out smoother and more enjoyable for everyone. - Satpreet Singh, Pinnacle Digital Advisors
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. Guiding Patron’s Meal Selections
Restaurants could leverage AI to help patrons choose their meals. Restaurants could develop interactive digital menus with a built-in virtual assistant that will provide information about ingredients, nutritional value and allergen warnings in real time and entertain or survey customers while they’re waiting for their orders. This would free up the waitstaff’s time and help marketers collect customer insights. - Konstantin Klyagin, Redwerk
4. Identifying Repeat Customers For Enhanced Service
Restaurants can use AI devices with facial recognition capabilities to identify repeat customers. Using data collected about these patrons’ past orders, preferences and behaviors, AI can help restaurants anticipate their needs and personalize their experiences, even with the high turnover of human staff members. However, patrons need to be informed about, and consent to, the collection and use of this data. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society
5. Reducing The Number Of Unsatisfactory Orders
In restaurants, patrons return food to the kitchen for various reasons—the food is under- or overcooked, the order is wrong, and so on. If such data were entered into an app, AI could analyze the kinds of food that are frequently returned and why, thereby formulating effective, data-driven solutions to reduce the number of dissatisfied customers and improve the overall quality of meals. - Syed Ahmed, Act-On Software
6. Powering Food-Preparation Robots
Not only do service robots boost productivity within the restaurant industry, but they also unleash cost-effective capabilities for employers looking to serve consumers and support the human workforce. For example, White Castle has introduced Flippy 2, a fully autonomous bot that uses computer vision to identify menu items and cooking times and can handle culinary tasks such as deep frying. - Jeff Wong, EY
7. Automating Order Processing
The implementation of AI-driven customer service systems and automated order processing could transform the day-to-day operations of restaurants. This could mean a shift for restaurant workers toward more strategic and creative tasks, such as enhancing the dining experience, planning menus and creating marketing strategies. The overall impact would likely be positive—primarily, faster and more accurate order processing. - Phil Portman, Textdrip
8. Freeing Up Chefs’ Time
AI-powered kitchens could predict demand, personalize menus and automate tasks, freeing chefs for creative roles. This might lead to fewer prep staff, but chefs could focus on artistry and customer interaction, enhancing the dining experience. Patrons might enjoy quicker service and more unique offerings. - Shelli Brunswick, SB Global LLC
9. Modeling Patrons’ Preferences
Restaurants strive to anticipate the desires of their clientele. Imagine using predictive AI solutions and data lakes to sift through and model clientele preferences. Sure, patrons may have privacy concerns. But most folks will gladly give up a bit of data for a unique dining experience, as long as you pitch it right. - James Stanger, CompTIA
10. Providing Unique Menus For Each Customer
Imagine pulling up to a drive-through. You may notice that an AI bot is speaking, not a real person. What you won’t notice, however, is that there is a camera identifying your license plate number and associated customer account. The items on the menu will be personalized for you—even the prices may change. Restaurants will use AI to not only interact with you, but also maximize ticket sizes and increase revenue. - Nicholas Domnisch, EES Health
11. Adjusting Energy Usage
AI could optimize energy usage in restaurants by adjusting the lighting and climate based on occupancy and weather data. This would reduce both costs and the restaurant’s carbon footprint, creating a comfortable environment for patrons while allowing the staff to focus more on customer service and sustainability efforts. - Marc Rutzen, HelloData.ai
12. Digitizing Recipes And Coaching Cooks
AI could digitize chefs’ treasured recipes, techniques and seasoning blends to spread knowledge across restaurants without losing nuance. Algorithmic assistants that have learned the subtle methods of top creators can then adaptively coach line cooks through voice prompts. This could democratize expertise to elevate consistency while freeing head chefs to further push boundaries. - Marc Fischer, Dogtown Media LLC
13. Optimizing Supply Usage
AI can transform restaurants by streamlining kitchen operations. AI-driven systems can optimize ingredient usage, reduce waste and enhance the efficiency of food preparation. For workers, this means less time spent on routine tasks and more time to focus on creativity and customer service. Patrons will benefit from consistent food quality and potentially faster service, enhancing their dining experience. - Ryan Lasmaili, Vaultree

title: To shush AI Act critics, the EU fine-tunes innovation pitch
text:
BRUSSELS — The European Union has a message for its artificial intelligence naysayers: It can innovate as well as regulate.
The EU was quick out of the gate to regulate AI — it was one of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's key political promises back in 2019. But as the bloc puts the finishing touches on its AI rulebook, some critics worry the new rules could hamper Europe's competitive position against the United States, China and other rivals.
To assuage those fears, some EU executives — including von der Leyen — have started talking up their efforts to give European startups what they need to keep up in the global AI race, such as staff, money, data and computing power.
This week, the European Commission is set to present a plan, obtained by POLITICO, to link the bloc's AI startups with European supercomputers, addressing the companies' need for vast amounts of computing power to stay competitive.
You may like
Earlier Commission agendas had the plan down for February 21, suggesting that the EU executive accelerated its AI innovation efforts — just as EU member countries are deliberating whether to green-light the bloc's proposed Artificial Intelligence Act.
Commission chief von der Leyen gave a sneak peek of the plan to a global audience last week during a talk at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.
In an address that was starry-eyed about the future of tech, von der Leyen said, "AI is also a very significant opportunity, if used in a responsible way," calling herself a "tech optimist."
Von der Leyen also singled out an area where Europe should lead the pack: industrial AI. During this mandate, the Commission has already laid the groundwork to improve the sharing of machine-generated data, which could prove to be key for automation and industries' use of AI.
The new plan to provide startups and SMEs access to European supercomputers is similar to what "Microsoft is doing for ChatGPT by running it on its own supercomputers," von der Leyen added, referring to the corporate front-runners in the global AI race.
The innovation push's timing might not be coincidental, though.
EU legislators are in the final stages of their work on the AI Act. Some member countries, especially France, attacked the bill in the lead-up to and aftermath of a political deal that was struck in early December, claiming it could discourage European innovation in the flourishing field.
France was concerned that the possible introduction of new compliance rules for so-called foundation models — advanced AI architectures similar to that which powers OpenAI’s ChatGPT — would hamper its national champions, such as open-source AI company Mistral. Germany and Italy also shared these worries.
In November last year, Berlin, Paris and Rome circulated a statement calling for looser requirements for foundation models than those envisioned in some versions of the AI law drafted by European policymakers under the Spanish EU Council presidency.
The AI Act’s final text, penned in late December under Spain’s stewardship, which POLITICO has seen, largely cleaves to the demands, replacing the concept of foundation models with the wider category of general-purpose AI — as the three countries had requested.
Still, France has remained noncommittal on whether it would back the final version of the AI Act.
At the same time, the EU's innovation push isn't entirely isolated from discussions on how to mitigate AI's risks — a reminder that, while a focus on competitiveness has long been in the ether, regulatory considerations are always part of the conversation.
A provisional header of the plan specifies that access to European supercomputers is for "ethical and responsible artificial intelligence startups." How ethics and responsibility are defined remains to be seen.
European Innovation Commissioner Iliana Ivanova, who was also present in Davos, told POLITICO that, indeed, a "balanced approach" was needed.
"Obviously, the contribution[s] of AI and supercomputing to increase productivity, increase efficiency and bring much higher efficiency gains are very clear," she said. At the same time, "We have to ... look at the ethical aspects [and] the human centricity of these projects."
Gian Volpicelli contributed reporting.
This article was updated to include a link to the draft EU communication obtained by POLITICO.

title: AI-generated robocall impersonates Biden in an apparent attempt to suppress votes in New Hampshire
text:
AI-generated robocall impersonates Biden in an apparent attempt to suppress votes in New Hampshire
The New Hampshire attorney general’s office says it is investigating reports of an apparent robocall that used artificial intelligence to mimic President Joe Biden’s voice and discourage voters in the state from participating in Tuesday’s primary election
The New Hampshire attorney general's office on Monday said it was investigating reports of an apparent robocall that used artificial intelligence to mimic President Joe Biden's voice and discourage voters in the state from coming to the polls during Tuesday's primary election.
Attorney General John Formella said the recorded message, which was sent to multiple voters on Sunday, appears to be an illegal attempt to disrupt and suppress voting. He said voters "should disregard the contents of this message entirely.”
A recording of the call reviewed by The Associated Press generates a voice similar to Biden’s and employs his often-used phrase, “What a bunch of malarkey.” It then tells the listener to “save your vote for the November election.”
“Voting this Tuesday only enables the Republicans in their quest to elect Donald Trump again,” the voice mimicking Biden says. “Your vote makes a difference in November, not this Tuesday.”
It is not true that voting in Tuesday's primary precludes voters from casting a ballot in November's general election. Biden is not campaigning in New Hampshire and his name will not appear on Tuesday's primary ballot after he elevated South Carolina to the lead-off position for the Democratic primaries, but his allies are running a write-in campaign for him in the state.
It's not known who is behind the calls, though they falsely showed up to recipients as coming from the personal cellphone number of Kathy Sullivan, a former state Democratic Party chair who helps run Granite for America, a super-PAC supporting the Biden write-in campaign.
Sullivan said she alerted law enforcement and issued a complaint to the attorney general after multiple voters in the state reported receiving the call Sunday night.
“This call links back to my personal cell phone number without my permission," she said in a statement. "It is outright election interference, and clearly an attempt to harass me and other New Hampshire voters who are planning to write-in Joe Biden on Tuesday.”
It was unclear how many people received the call but a spokesperson for Sullivan said she heard from at least a dozen people who received it. The attorney general’s office encouraged anyone who has received the call to email the state Justice Department’s election law unit.
Gail Huntley, a 73-year-old Democrat in Hancock, New Hampshire, who plans to write in Biden’s name on Tuesday, said she received the call at about 6:25 p.m. on Sunday.
She instantly recognized the voice as belonging to Biden but quickly realized it was a scam because what he was saying didn’t make sense. Initially, she figured his words were taken out of context.
“I didn’t think about it at the time that it wasn’t his real voice. That’s how convincing it was,” she said, adding that she is appalled but not surprised that AI-generated fakes like this are spreading in her state.
Biden’s campaign manager, Julie Chavez Rodriguez, said in a statement that the campaign is “actively discussing additional actions to take immediately.”
“Spreading disinformation to suppress voting and deliberately undermine free and fair elections will not stand, and fighting back against any attempt to undermine our democracy will continue to be a top priority for this campaign,” she said.
The apparent attempt at voter suppression using rapidly advancing generative AI technology is one example of what experts warn will make 2024 a year of unprecedented election disinformation around the world.
Generative AI deepfakes already have appeared in campaign ads in the 2024 presidential race, and the technology has been misused to spread misinformation in multiple elections across the globe over the past year, from Slovakia to Indonesia and Taiwan.
“We have been concerned that generative AI would be weaponized in the upcoming election and we are seeing what is surely a sign of things to come,” said Hany Farid, an expert in digital forensics at the University of California, Berkeley, who reviewed the call recording and confirmed it is a relatively low-quality AI fake.
As AI technology improves, the federal government is still scrambling to address it. Congress has yet to pass legislation seeking to regulate the industry’s role in politics despite some bipartisan support. The Federal Election Commission is weighing public comments on a petition for it to regulate AI deepfakes in campaign ads.
Though the use of generative AI to influence elections is relatively new, “robocalls and dirty tricks go back a long ways," said David Becker, a former U.S. Department of Justice attorney and election law expert who now leads the Center for Election Innovation and Research.
He said it's hard to determine whether the main intent of the New Hampshire calls was to suppress voting or simply to “continue the process of getting Americans to untether themselves from fact and truth regarding our democracy.”
“They don’t need to convince us that what they’re saying, the lies they’re telling, are true,” he said. "They just need to convince us that there is no truth, that you can’t believe anything you’re told.”
Katie Dolan, a spokeswoman for the campaign of Rep. Dean Phillips of Minnesota, who is challenging Biden in the Democratic primary, said Phillips’ team was not involved and only found out about the deepfake attempt when a reporter called seeking comment.
“Any effort to discourage voters is disgraceful and an unacceptable affront to democracy,” Dolan said in a statement. “The potential use of AI to manipulate voters is deeply disturbing.”
The Trump campaign said it had nothing to do with the recording but declined further comment.
___
Associated Press writer Christina A. Cassidy contributed to this report from Atlanta.

title: Dell Technologies BrandVoice: Technology-Inspired Changes: A Look At What’s Coming In 2024
text:
While short-term focus is vital during challenging macroeconomic times, these technology-based trends will (and should) get business attention in 2024.
In a recent keynote, Dell Technologies CTO John Roese said “Vision without execution is just a dream.” Looking at the year ahead, that’s an apt way to set the stage for 2024.
During challenging macroeconomic times, organizations must manage budgets more closely. Organizations often focus more on shorter-term tactics that are immediately deployable and top technology priorities that best serve their customers, both of which help stabilize their business through market turbulence.
As a technology marketer, I am excited about what I expect to see in 2024—I anticipate a slower start to get through the macroeconomic challenges, then on to sunnier skies later in the year. So, here’s my January reset, reflect and refresh exercise from a trends and technology perspective. I bet you can already guess the first one…
It’s time for tactics
While organizational vision remains important, it’s time for tactics. Out of necessity, organizations will focus more on pressing tactical priorities that can deliver speedy outcomes. Thought leadership ideas and longer-term optimization and refinement projects—such as removing technical debt or breaking down internal siloes—will garner some attention but be trumped by projects that deliver near-term ROI.
Artificial intelligence (AI) will continue to go mainstream
Thanks to the rapid and pervasive adoption of generative AI large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, AI is more widely understood, relatable, accessible and familiar, catalyzing a newfound passion for AI.
I see AI moving from an arcane art practiced by a select few highly-trained specialists to an everyday toolset embraced by the masses. From businesses to students, families planning vacations and everyone in between, AI will begin to permeate our daily lives.
In business, AI’s relatable familiarity will cause a big increase in AI investment to fuel applications such as analysis of the world through computer vision, pattern detection and digital twins. Although AI is not as readily approachable as generative AI, I believe that AI will begin to feel like an everyday tool and become table stakes for all businesses.
Edge will gain even more momentum
As AI moves mainstream in business, it will elevate customer expectations, raising the bar for personalized, relevant experiences and moving them from best-in-class standouts to mainstream occurrences. To run, these AI deployments and applications need access to real-time, streaming data—and lots of it. That data is found at the edge, where the majority of new data is generated. While some of the edge’s data will be backhauled to clouds, most of it will be processed at the edge due to speed, scale and security concerns that stem from moving data.
We will see the emergence of modern edges as multicloud infrastructure extends into stores, hospitals and factories. Today, these solutions are specific to each cloud workload, necessitating cloud-specific service and hardware deployments. However, modern edge locations can run a common multicloud platform that operates any software-defined edge workload to support any cloud, IoT, or IT system, greatly simplifying edge deployments. Dell NativeEdge does just that, and I’m excited to see it help organizations modernize, streamline and elevate their edge approach.
Multicloud will pick up speed
Another piece of wisdom from Roese’s keynote is about multicloud expansion. He stated, “Modern IT is implemented using cloud operations principles. Whether that’s at the edge, in a private environment, public cloud, co-location or SaaS…”
Organizations use the IT environments that have the resources they need. That means companies will train AI where they have access to the best data science features – typically in the cloud or data center. They will operate their business where they can most efficiently run tracking and reporting, processing slower or smaller data sets in the cloud and faster data sets at the edge. Multicloud will stitch together all these environments into a cohesive, comprehensive and functional IT system.
Organizations will focus on sustainability priorities
In the year ahead, AI acceleration will also bring renewed attention to sustainability. Here’s why. As AI moves into mainstream adoption in 2024, we’ll see an increasing awareness of and focus on managing AI’s colossal power needs. Consequently, organizations will pay more attention to how their workloads are powered - some from environmental concerns and some from pragmatic cost and risk control. For either motivation, the results will reprioritize sustainability initiatives overall.
Bringing it all together
By the end of 2024, conversations will focus more on a short but actionable list of projects. Organizations will focus on how those projects are driving the business forward using data locally and across the multicloud and more clearly defining how they connect to the company’s AI progress while accounting for sustainability. Companies will move from longer-term dreams to present-day realities as they focus on generating immediate results while investing strategically, gaining forward momentum for a stronger future.

title: ‘True Detective: Night Country’ Used AI Generated Art In Its Latest Episode
text:
In a bizarre turn of events, it turns out that the creative team behind HBO’s True Detective: Night Country have included at least one AI-generated poster in the show’s second episode.
When Detective Navarro (Kali Reis) interviews a local miner about the case she and Liz Danvers (Jodi Foster) are investigating, she visits the man in his shabby apartment. On the wall are two very peculiar posters.
The first is of the K-Pop band IVE and some folks online are saying it’s a legit poster. I can’t find it on an image search but that doesn’t mean it isn’t real. It does appear to have both a legit symbol for the band in the upper right corner and the same words and font at the bottom that say ‘LOVE DIVE’ which you can find online pretty easily.
Why a grown man in Ennis, Alaska has a K-Pop poster is another matter entirely, though showrunner Issa Lopez has said there was a line about his daughter liking K-Pop that was cut because it didn’t work in the scene. Fair enough.
The second poster is clearly AI. It says ‘METAL at the top, though the font is distorted in that very obviously AI way. This band called just METAL, apparently, is on a U.S. Tour. In yellow bubbles at the bottom, you can see the words 1ST LIVE and 2ST LIVE. Yes, 2ST, not 2ND.
You can also buy this work of, um, well not art but something art-adjacent, online for yourself right here. Hooboy.
Lopez has replied to a handful of tweets about this poster on Twitter. “The story behind this poster is so long, it would require its own season of TD,” she replied to one poster.
Another tweet:
“The idea is that it's so sad up there that some kid with AI made the posters for a loser Metal festival for boomers,” Lopez replies. “It was discussed. Ad nauseam.”
But . . . this doesn’t make any sense. A kid in Ennis is printing full-sized color posters of bad AI art? Why is this more effective than just having a KISS poster on the wall? We—as viewers—are supposed to intuit all this from seeing an AI poster? Wouldn’t the idea that he’s a washed out dude stuck in the past be conveyed perfectly fine simply by having some aged rocker poster that isn’t, well, whatever this is?
Nothing else in Night Country deals with the topic of AI at all (so far) so it’s kind of hard to make sense out of this explanation.
I’m not someone who decries AI in all its forms, mind you. I think it can be fun to play around with AI art generators or ChatGPT just for fun. But I can’t condone using AI posters like this when a real artist could be used for a major, big-budget TV program. All these needle drops—Billie Eilish, Florence and the Machine etc.—but you can’t just hire an artist to make a poster or use a real poster and pay whatever licensing fee that requires?
Oh well. I’m sure the hardest of hardcore fans will find ways to spin this into some kind of purposeful thing, a part of the bigger mystery or something along those lines. I think it’s in keeping with the rest of the season so far: Cheap, generic and nothing like True Detective.

title: An Eight Minute Meeting App, Execs Go Cautious On AI And More
text:
This is the published version of Forbes' Future of Work newsletter, which offers the latest news for chief human resources officers and other talent managers on disruptive technologies, managing the workforce and trends in the remote work debate. Click here to get it delivered to your inbox every Monday!
Early in the pandemic, there was a lot of talk about working in the metaverse. Or alternatively, some video-game like version of the office, where an online avatar would scoot from one on-screen room to another, passing by digital water coolers and pixelated ferns, perhaps with a video bubble following along. Neither idea has caught on widely, and return-to-office mandates aren’t exactly encouraging their use.
But serial entrepreneur Howard Lerman, who cofounded publicly traded online marketing platform Yext, has a different idea: A virtual HQ, but pare it down. Prioritize audio. Do away with avatars and video bubbles. The result is Roam, a startup that exited its invite-only beta period last week, and that I profiled in a story here.
One of the most interesting things Lerman shared with me is something that happens when companies start using their app. The interface is set up visually like a map, emphasizing presence—who’s available, who’s not—encouraging impromptu “knocks” on office doors rather than scheduled 30-minute Zoom calls. As a result, organizations often see their average number of meetings go up after starting to use Roam, but the average time spent in them go down. “It’s kind of a funny thing,” Lerman told me. “I don't know if it’s nature or what, but somehow most companies see average meeting times of right around eight minutes” after using Roam.
Whether you really need an app to get you there or not, it’s a reminder that a lot of meetings could have been an email—or at least an eight-minute check-in when you drop by someone’s office, pick up the phone for a quick call, or hop on a Slack huddle or a tool like Roam to have a brief chat. Finding ways to break up the 30-minute meeting’s stronghold on your calendar—and your organization’s—can go a long way to working more efficiently.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
The World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland took place last week (if you’re curious what it’s like, don’t miss Keith Ferrazzi’s tips on becoming a conference commando), and AI, unsurprisingly, was the buzzword everywhere at the annual confab. But amid all of the talk—and despite AI’s rampant adoption—new surveys by consulting firms Oliver Wyman, Boston Consulting Group and Accenture show executives feel AI has yet to progress past the hype, Emmy Lucas reports.
In a survey of 1,400 executives by the Boston Consulting Group released at Davos, 66% of leaders say they are uncertain or outright dissatisfied with their company’s progress on AI so far. Among white-collar workers, 30% of employees say generative AI has not changed their productivity, a global survey of 25,000 professionals by Oliver Wyman Forum found. And nearly three-quarters of executives say they are purposely exercising restraint with generative AI investments due to societal pressures for responsible AI, according to a report from Accenture covered earlier this month by contributor Joe McKendrick (he wrote about another report from Accenture last week).
HUMAN CAPITAL
A new year hasn’t stopped the parade of tech layoffs. Wayfair CEO Niraj Shah—who a week earlier urged employees to work “long hours”—told employees Friday the company is slashing 1,650 jobs, or 13% of its workforce, in an effort to “position the company both now and over the long term.” Google, Amazon, Macy’s and Twitch also recently announced plans to cut jobs, raising questions about whether the tide on job cuts will really turn in 2024. New Forbes contributor Q Hamirani—the former global head of remote work at Airbnb and current chief people officer at Paper—writes about how the job cuts are impacting tech HR departments.
POLICY & PRACTICE
Forbes’ Kelly Phillips Erb reports on a new bipartisan tax proposal that would restore bonus depreciation and put an early end to the Employee Retention Credit (ERC), among other changes. Titled "The Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024," the plan is expected to cost around $78 billion. Of note for HR leaders: The proposal would put an end to the beleaguered Employee Retention Credit—or ERC—program as of Jan. 31, 2024. Intended to aid businesses that were shut down or experienced a specific decline in gross receipts during Covid, the ERC program has experienced a “tsunami” of claims that appeared fraudulent, IRS Commissioner Danny Werfel said.
END OF AN ERA
Billionaire Sheryl Sandberg, the former chief operating officer at Meta, is leaving the company’s board of directors after more than a decade. Sandberg, who served on Meta’s board for 12 years, long served as a voice—at times a controversial one—on women, work and how they can advance in their careers. Her book Lean In: Women, Work, and the Will to Lead, published in 2013, sparked debates about how much the lack of female leaders was due to women’s so-called “will to lead,” or the obstacles and cultures put in their way by the organizations in which they work.
WHAT’S NEXT: GREENHOUSE CHIEF PEOPLE OFFICER DONALD KNIGHT
Donald Knight is the chief people officer at Greenhouse, the “hiring worktech” company and applicant tracking system, giving him a view into not only how his own company recruits candidates and manages hybrid work, but how other companies are doing the same. Forbes spoke with Knight about the generational aspect of remote work, AI and new tech tools on his radar. The excerpts below from our conversation have been edited for length and clarity.
There’s a lot of talk about 2024 being a year when people who haven’t yet gone back to the office finally will. Greenhouse lets people choose where they work. Do you think that's actually going to change much this year?
I'm a numbers guy first, so I always try to go to the numbers. If you look at the percentage of CEOs that announced retirements last year, we're seeing this great passing of the torch. We will also see that disruption in the workplace. Gen Z will make up 30% of the workplace in 2036. That’s six years from now. That’s not that far.
So you think the remote work discussion is generational?
I think the numbers tell us that generationally, we saw Gen Z, and now Gen Alpha—these people were going to school from home. They were taking exams from home. Gaming is at an all time high—these kids are playing with kids in different states, in different countries. That is their normal.
For my grandfather, working one job for almost 40 years was his normal. Today, the average employee is going to work at least ten jobs [over the course of their career]. It's a different dynamic. I think that's the discussion that most chief people officers are having with their executive leadership team. The dynamics are just different now.
There’s so much attention to the issue of flexible or hybrid work. What’s missing in the discussion?
I think we've gotten away from thinking that you can have people conversations through a business lens. Most people think you're either only doing stuff for people or you're only doing things for the business. I reject that notion. I believe profitability happens at the intersection of growth and efficiency. People want to grow in their careers. They also want to take care of the people who matter the most to them. If they have to worry about the things that are happening outside of the workplace, it affects the way that they show up inside the workplace.
How do you see AI impacting recruiting?
Every company has to take AI seriously. The dynamics of the actual labor market are changing, and how I communicate to the generations that are coming is very different. … AI can be used to create more of that content [for career sites].
The second one for me is around categorization. How are you categorizing hires in your applicant tracking system or in your human capital management system? Think about the silver medalists [the candidates who were great but didn’t quite get the job]. Do you have a way to intentionally go back to them? And then, for the people I offer a job to but they decline, how do I make sure, two months from now or two years from now when I have a more elevated senior position, I go back to them?
Then there’s categorizing why people declined. Typically, that's a human doing that. It's manual work. I think dashboards like that'll be phenomenal.
What kind of new AI tools are you seeing help with the interviewing process?
If you're looking at high-growth or high-volume hiring, we're seeing people use video as a way of doing the initial screen. There's a company called WedgeHR for video recruiting and video screening. They say they can cut the screening time in half. The second one would be a company like BrightHire, which we’ve partnered with. If I were interviewing you for a role, it can summarize all of the notes from the interview so you can be more [engaged] watching it, and then you can go back and press the replay. It allows you to populate our scorecard or other ATS scorecards quickly because it's constantly capturing notes.

QUIZ

The test will be taken on a computer or tablet, is shorter than the physical version, and is adaptive so the questions in the latter part of the test will vary depending on how well test-takers perform earlier.
